b: Janus Films will become the North American distributor of Frederick Wiseman’s complete body of work starting January 1, as first reported by Variety. The deal covers all 45 features that Wiseman produced, directed, and edited, from his 1967 debut, Titicut Follies, his exposé of a Massachusetts institution for the criminally insane, to 2023’s Menus-Plaisirs Les Troisgros, a look at a three-Michelin-star restaurant in central France.

Janus is licensing the films from Zipporah Films, the company Wiseman named for his wife, which remains their rights holder. Everything from Titicut Follies through 2007’s State Legislature will be available in 4K restorations, while the later films, beginning with 2009’s La Danse: The Paris Opera Ballet, will be offered in their original digital formats. “We’re looking forward to presenting these monumental works, theatrically, to new audiences across the country,” said Peter Becker, president of Janus and its sister label, the Criterion Collection.

Those restorations were already on Wiseman’s mind when Slant’s Patrick Preziosi spoke with him in 2022 about A Couple. “At this moment, I’m actually involved in color grading a lot of my older films that were shot on film, those that unfortunately can’t be shown in most theaters nowadays,” he said, adding that restoring them in 4K would be “at least a six-month project.”

Wiseman, who died in February at 96, spent nearly six decades planting his camera inside hospitals, high schools, police precincts, and city halls and recording the everyday workings of power and care at length, without narration or interviews. He preferred to call his films “reality fictions,” and he described his process to us in 2012 as discovering each film in the editing room, a job he never handed off. “I’ve edited all my films myself,” he said in that interview, conducted on the occasion of Crazy Horse’s U.S. release. He received an honorary Oscar in 2016.

That method yielded some of the most expansive portraits of civic life ever filmed. Reviewing 2020’s City Hall, Keith Uhlich wrote that its provocations “emerge from an observational tranquility that is uniquely Frederick Wiseman’s own,” while Chuck Bowen called Ex Libris: New York Public Library “a college course and a guided tour wedded together as a work of prismatic humanist art.” Wiseman also bristled at being pigeonholed as a maker of issue films, and his later work ranged from London’s National Gallery to the Paris Opera Ballet. As he put it [[clarify that this is in the interview with Budd Wilkins from 2012]], “A movie about a ballet company or a theater company is just as much a social subject as a movie about a welfare center.”
